newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy navy says unlikely many Albanians drowned.
newsitem.headline: Italy navy says unlikely many Albanians drowned.

text.p: Italy said on Saturday that it was possible more than four people had died when an Albanian boat collided with a navy corvette and sank in the Adriatic but it doubted survivors' accounts that up to 100 may have perished.

Admiral Angelo Mariani, the navy chief of staff, told a news conference in Rome that four Albanians -- three women and a man -- had died in the incident in international waters on Friday evening and 34 people had been rescued.
He said the search for survivors was continuing.

"I cannot exclude unfortunately that there were other people on board but I don't think there could have been too many more below deck," Mariani said. "It seems exaggerated to me that there could have been 100 people on board."
Survivors arriving in the southern port of Brindisi during the night feared many more had perished.
"More than 50 of us died," one Albanian man shouted to reporters gathered on the dock.
Mariani said that such a figure was unlikely since the boat, an ageing Russian-built harbour patrol craft, was about 20 metres long and had limited space below deck.
He added that the ship had stayed afloat for about an hour before sinking.
In response to a question, he acknowledged that people with no seafaring experience caught below deck could have have had difficulties reaching the surface.
Officers on the corvette Sibilla had seen no sign of passengers below deck through the boat's portholes.
Survivors taken to Brindisi told reporters variously that there were between 70 and more than 100 people on the ship at the time. A number of passengers were children, they said.
The Albanian boat sank after being approached by the Sibilla which was seeking to head it off from Italian waters in accordance with government orders.
The defence ministry said on Friday that the Albanian boat, with about 30 people visible on deck, had collided with the Sibilla after cutting across its bows abruptly.
Italy, concerned that many Albanian refugees are looking for a better life abroad rather than fleeing real danger, has ordered the navy to patrol the Adriatic to halt the flow.
The deterrence operation, introduced on Monday, involves intercepting Albanian ships before they enter Italian waters and then advising them to turn back for home.
Mariani defended the navy action and the Sibilla's captain Fabrizio Laudadio, saying the patrols would continue.
"As far as we are concerned, it was they who hit us," the admiral said of the incident.
"The accident happened because the Albanian ship behaved in an unpredictable and irresponsible way."
Mariani, who met the Albanian ambassador to Rome, said Tirana had informed Italy that the Albanian boat was piloted by "local criminals" with no seafaring experience.
"Obviously the person at the helm did not know what he was doing or he made a big error of evaluation to think that he could cut off the corvette," he said.
Some politicians criticised the navy actions while others pointed the finger at Albania. Fringe groups called for the resignation of Defence Minister Beniamino Andreatta.
Cosmo Ruppi, the Roman Catholic archbishop of the southern Italian town of Lecce, said the tragedy "weighed on the consciences of men" and could have been avoided.

More than 13,000 Albanians have reached Italy in the past two weeks on a flotilla of ancient and rusty boats after rebels in the impoverished Balkan country took control of towns in the south in an armed insurrection.
The sinking was the first incident involving fatalities since the exodus of Albanians began on March 13.
